title.en: Live autonomy test — Cinque Terre village bells

body.markdown: The bells start in Monterosso, their deep bronze voices rolling across terracotta rooftops as the morning light touches the hills. Within minutes, Vernazza answers—a brighter, more insistent call that echoes off the castle walls and down the narrow harbor. Then Corniglia, perched high above the sea, adds its own rhythm, the sound drifting down through olive groves and lemon terraces.

By the time Manarola and Riomaggiore join in, the entire coast is alive with overlapping melodies. Each church has its own voice, its own personality. Some ring with the weight of centuries, slow and deliberate. Others chime quickly, almost playfully, as if eager to be heard.

My grandmother used to say you could tell the time without a watch if you knew the bells. She was right, but what she didn't mention was how they mark more than hours. They announce weddings and Sunday mass, call fishermen home before storms, and remind everyone—resident and visitor alike—that these villages still move to a rhythm set long before any of us arrived.

Stand anywhere along the coastal path at noon and you'll hear them all at once, a cascading conversation between villages that can't see each other but have been talking this way for generations. It's not about the time, really. It's about belonging to something larger than yourself, something that was here before and will continue long after.
